To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
leg conformation, litter size at farrowing, and farm management are the major factors that impact on length of productive life.
sow's origin parity, number of pigs in the litter of birth, and leg conformation have no effect on LPL in crossbred sows.
the parity of the piglets within a litter and the number of piglets within that litter have no impact on LPL in a crossbred (Landrance × LargeWhite or LargeWhite × Landrance) population.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the genetic aspects of LPL in crossbred sows, but it is important to note that the environment and management play major roles in LPL, and thus the genetic improvement of LPL is only one of several important aspects of improving sow productivity.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sow's own litter size at birth is not a factor affecting the LPL, but the parity of the sow's litter at birth and the litter size at first parity are factors affecting the LPL.

sows with better leg conformation, born in litters of smaller size and born later in parity, will remain productive for a longer period of time than those with poorer leg scores, born in livers of larger size, and born earlier in parity.
LPL is not affected by the parity of the birth litter or the number of pigs born in the same litter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
sows that have been in larger litters and have been born earlier in the parity have longer LPL.
the best way to improve sow longevity would be to improve the sow's own prolific potential and the sow's ability to produce piglets which grow well and are healthy.
the best leg score is a good indicator of future longevity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sows should be culled based on their performance and longevity, not on their litter size or age.
